The false premise is the expensive failure

Strategy · AI

In short: AI systems have become good at saying "I don't know". They remain bad at saying "that's not right any more". The second failure is the one that costs money, and the fix is a cheap check almost nobody runs.

Key points

  • False-premise errors are not hallucinations; every fact may be correct while the answer accepts an outdated assumption.
  • A premise check extracts the question's presuppositions and checks each against current records with status and validity dates.
  • If a premise is contradicted, say so first with the record and date, then answer the right question.
  • The check costs one extra call and a few hundred tokens per question.
  • Build a twenty-question false-premise evaluation from your own superseded records and report the correction rate every release.

In one 2026 benchmark, a widely used memory layer abstained correctly on 99.3% of questions where the evidence was missing. On questions that carried a false premise, it corrected the premise 14.6% of the time.

Read those two numbers together. The industry has largely solved the failure everyone worried about in 2023: confidently answering when nothing supports the answer. It has barely touched a subtler one. When a question smuggles in an assumption that the record contradicts, the system answers the question as asked.

What this looks like inside a firm

An analyst asks: "Given that the client's loan condition was waived last year, what should we watch this quarter?" If the waiver was reversed in July, the record knows. But the question presupposes the waiver, and the system will usually produce a fluent, well-sourced answer about monitoring a waived loan condition.

A relationship manager asks: "Since procurement approved the budget, what's the fastest path to signature?" The budget approval was a forecast, never confirmed. The answer is a confident plan built on nothing.

These are not hallucinations in the usual sense. Every fact in the answer may be correct. The error is in what the answer accepted without checking.

Why people do not catch it either

Questions from senior people carry premises that junior people rarely challenge. A system that would push back on a false premise is, among other things, a way to correct a senior colleague without the politics. That is a real organisational benefit, and it only exists if the system is built to do it.

The premise check

The fix is a step before answering, and it is cheap to build.

  1. Extract the presuppositions in the question. Models are good at this when asked directly: "What does this question assume to be true?"
  2. Check each presupposition against current records, using status and validity dates.
  3. If any is contradicted or superseded, say so first, with the record and date, before answering anything.
  4. Then answer the question that should have been asked, or ask whether the user still wants the original.

The check costs one extra call and a few hundred tokens per question. On questions that touch live decisions, that is an easy trade.

Test for it explicitly

Most evaluation sets test whether a system finds the right answer. Add a set that tests whether it refuses a wrong question. Your own superseded records are the ideal source: take twenty views the organisation once held and later reversed, and write questions that assume the old view. Score how often the system pushes back. Expect a low number at first.

In practice

  • Add a premise-check step before answers on any question tied to a live decision.
  • Build a twenty-question false-premise evaluation from your own superseded records.
  • Report the false-premise correction rate alongside accuracy, every release.
  • Make the pushback polite and specific: the record, the date, the change.

What would prove this wrong. Systems without a premise check correcting false premises at rates close to their abstention rates on independent tests. Then the gap has closed on its own and the extra step is redundant.

Common questions

What is a false-premise error in AI?

When a question assumes something the record contradicts and the system answers the question as asked. Every fact in the answer may be correct; the error is what it accepted without checking.

How can I stop an AI assistant from answering questions based on outdated assumptions?

Add a premise check before answering: extract what the question assumes, check each assumption against current records, and flag any that are contradicted or superseded before answering.

How do I test whether my AI system catches false premises?

Take twenty views your organisation once held and later reversed, write questions that assume the old view, and score how often the system pushes back. Expect a low number at first.
